# Born in the Nest: full text

> US-focused education about birth choices (home birth, birth centers, hospitals), fear of childbirth and first-time mom choices. Education only, not medical advice. Source: https://borninthenest.com

## Home birth & birth center FAQ · Born in the Nest
URL: https://borninthenest.com/faq.html
Answers to your birth questions: home birth, home birth vs birth center, finding a midwife, home birth cost, fear of childbirth and first-time mom choices.

FAQ
Answers to your birth questions
Home birth, birth centers, midwives and fear of birth, answered honestly.

These are the questions I hear most, and the ones I wish I'd asked before my first birth. Each answer is short and honest, so you can read more and take it to your midwife or doctor.

Jump to a question

What are my options for where to give birth in the US?
You can plan to give birth at home with a midwife, in a freestanding birth center, or in a hospital. You can choose wherever you want to give birth. It's your choice.

Most US babies are born in hospitals, so if you've never heard much about the other two options, you're not alone.

What are the alternatives to a hospital birth?
The two main alternatives are a planned home birth and a birth center birth. Both are usually led by midwives, and planned with a clear path to a hospital if more help is needed.

A birth center is an inviting place you get to know really well, because you go there for your visits every month, so it feels a bit like a home away from home. It's beautiful and warm. Nobody rushes you, it's calm, and there are no harsh bright lights. And just like at home, you can invite whoever you want to your birth. If a hospital is the right place for you, many hospitals also offer midwife care.

Read more: Birth center vs hospital: what's the difference?

What should I know about home birth?
Home birth is an amazing option. Before you rule it out, go talk to midwives and other moms who have actually done it, and see if it's the right fit for you. For me, after giving birth in a hospital, I knew there had to be another option, because it just didn't feel like the right fit. A birth center and my midwives were one hundred percent the right fit. Every time I walked in, I felt cared for and calm, instead of rushed like in a busy hospital.

What should I know about home birth with a first baby?
Every pregnancy is different, and with a first baby there's so much that's new. Many first-time moms also love the idea of a birth center, a calm, home-like middle path.

A first labor may take time, which is why it's even more important to be somewhere you feel calm and loved, so you don't slow the process down. That's one reason a birth center can be a beautiful choice for a first baby. Many first-time moms do plan a home birth, and your midwife can help you weigh it for your own pregnancy.

Read more: Can I have a home birth with my first baby?

Home birth vs birth center: what's the difference?
With a home birth, your midwife comes to you. You labor in your own space, in your own bed or a birth pool, with only the people you choose. With a birth center, you go to a home-like place run by midwives, often with large beds and birth tubs, and with arrangements for transfer to a hospital when needed.

At home, everything happens on your terms: your own lights, your own food, your own space. In a hospital, things mostly happen on their terms.

Both are midwife-led. Choosing between them often comes down to where you feel most relaxed, how far you live from a hospital, and what's available near you.

Who is a good candidate for a home birth or birth center?
Any mom can be a fit for a home birth or a birth center. The only moms who aren't are the ones who want to give birth in a hospital no matter what. If you're curious, go talk to midwives who attend births at home or in a birth center and see if it feels right for you.

What happens if I need to go to the hospital during labor?
Just talk to your midwife. She'll have a plan, and she'll come with you, and that's the beautiful thing. Your midwives will know if anything is out of the norm, and they'll have a plan to get you to the hospital. That's how I felt with mine.

Read more: What happens if you need to transfer to the hospital during a home birth?

My partner is worried about home birth. What can help?
Most of the time the worry isn't really about how you'd get to the hospital. It's about seeing that birth is the most natural process, and women have been doing it for centuries. Meet your midwives together. They've done this so many times, and they can reassure your partner that there's nothing to be worried about.

Read more: My partner is worried about a home birth. What can help?

How do I tell my family I'm planning a home birth?
You don't have to tell anyone before the birth. I didn't, and that was okay. If you do share, tell them about the plan, not just the place: who your midwife is and that she has a transfer plan with a hospital. Listen to their worry, and remember you don't owe anyone a debate.

Read more: How do I tell my family I'm planning a home birth?

Who can be at my home birth?
Really anyone you want. Your partner, your other kids, your mom, your best friend. It's your birth, so you decide. Your older children can absolutely be part of it, which is so amazing, because that's something you usually can't have at a hospital. Some people even make it a party.

How do I find a midwife?
The easiest way is to search online for birth centers near you and midwives near you. The internet and AI are your friends here. Search online or ask an AI assistant for midwives, birth centers and hospitals near you, and read what other moms say in their reviews. I think those matter a lot, because real moms are sharing how it really went. Directories are a second option, but honestly they're so-so. Trust what other moms say.

Then book a consultation with two or three. Most offer one. Ask about her training and experience, who her backup is, her transfer plan and hospital, what equipment and medicines she brings, and what it costs. Then notice how you feel after talking with her. Do you feel loved, calm and heard? If you can't be yourself, can't ask any question you want, or feel pushed into certain things, that's a red flag, and you should pay attention to it.

Read more: How do I find a home birth midwife near me?

When do I need to decide where to give birth?
Starting early gives you the most choice, because some midwives and birth centers book up. But it's rarely too late to ask, and you can switch providers during pregnancy. Call, ask what's possible, and trust your gut.

Read more: When do I need to decide where to give birth? Can I switch?

What if I go past my due date?
My midwives could not care less about my due date. From the very beginning they told me the baby comes when the baby comes. So you have a birth month, but the exact day doesn't really matter. Hospitals often treat that date like a ticking clock. As you get close, they want you to come in, and if you go a day past it, everyone gets worried, and that can make you nervous too. With midwives, you just wait for your baby.

What should I ask on a birth center tour?
The most important thing is how you feel when you walk through that door. Do you feel calm? Are you surrounded by people who are nice and kind? Can you ask any question you want? That matters most. Once that feels right, ask all your other questions. If you can't be yourself, can't ask any question you want, or feel pushed into certain things, that's a red flag, and you should pay attention to it.

Ask who will care for you, what happens if you need a hospital, how long families stay after the birth, and what the price includes. Ask what they know about nutrition, sleep and wellbeing. Good pregnancy care is more than checkups. It includes how you eat, how you sleep and how you feel. Fueling your body is one of the most important things you can do during pregnancy, so your midwives should know a lot about it. If they can't really talk about nutrition, sleep and wellbeing, they're probably not the best fit.

Read more: What should I ask on a birth center tour?

How much does a home birth cost?
I paid $5,600 to my birth center midwives. I went there for all my visits, and my baby was born at home, because that's where I wanted to give birth. From what I saw, that's about average. Some midwives charged a little more and some a little less. It's usually one package fee that covers your prenatal visits, the birth and your care afterward. What you actually pay depends on your insurance, and many midwives will help you check your coverage, so it's a great question for your first visit. A hospital birth can cost a lot more or less depending on your plan. It depends on your insurance either way, so ask your insurer and each place for their prices.

Many places offer payment plans and loans, and they work with your insurance. You can often use your health savings account (HSA), and there may be tax deductions too, so really, all options are open.

Read more: How much does a home birth cost? · Does insurance cover a home birth?

I'm scared of giving birth. Is that normal?
Yes, it's very normal, and you're not alone. Fear of birth is so common because we grew up believing birth is scary. It is not. Your body is amazing, and it knows how to do this.

What helps: learning how birth really works, not the movie version. Labor comes in waves, and between contractions you get real breaks to rest and breathe. Nature doesn't want you to suffer. Knowing your options, a midwife or doctor who helps you feel calm, heard, and loved, and practicing calm breathing also help. If the fear is weighing on you, please tell your provider.

What does continuity of midwife care mean?
It means you're building your team. Think of it like a marathon: you assemble your team ahead of time, and on the day that matters, they're right there with you, and you trust them with everything. Imagine running a marathon without even knowing your team. You'd feel out of place. That's kind of how it felt for me at the hospital. With my home birth it was the opposite. I knew my team inside and out, and they knew me and my baby inside and out.

Can I use a birth pool or warm water in labor?
Warm water, such as a birth pool, tub or shower, is one comfort option many midwives and birth centers offer. Ask your midwife or birth center about birth pools and tubs. And you can have one at home too. My midwives brought a birth pool to my house.

What is hypnobirthing?
Hypnobirthing is a childbirth education approach that uses deep relaxation, slow breathing and visualization to help you stay calm in labor. When you're scared, your body tenses up, and that makes labor harder. When you feel calm and cared for, your body can relax and do its work. The best-known method is HypnoBirthing: The Mongan Method by Marie Mongan.

Is Born in the Nest medical advice?
No. Born in the Nest shares education and encouragement from one mom to another. It doesn't replace care from your midwife or doctor, so please talk to your provider about anything health-related.

## Touring a birth center: what to ask and how it should feel
URL: https://borninthenest.com/articles/birth-center-tour-questions.html
What to ask on a birth center tour: how the place feels, who will care for you, hospital transfer, how long you stay, and what the price includes.

Answers
🏡What should I ask on a birth center tour?

The short answer: The most important thing is how you feel when you walk through that door. Do you feel calm? Are you surrounded by people who are nice and kind? Can you ask any question you want? That matters most. Once that feels right, ask all your other questions.

By Sybille Mom of two · first birth in a hospital, second at home · Education only, not medical advice

A birth center tour is your chance to see the rooms, meet the people and ask anything you want. Here is what's worth asking, in plain words.

What is a birth center?

A birth center is an inviting place you get to know really well, because you go there for your visits every month, so it feels a bit like a home away from home. It's beautiful and warm. Nobody rushes you, it's calm, and there are no harsh bright lights. And just like at home, you can invite whoever you want to your birth.

Who will care for me?

Your midwives. That's what it's all about. Get to know them, spend time with them, and see if they're the right fit for you. The right midwife makes you feel calm, heard and loved, right from the first moment.

How does it feel?

This part matters as much as the answers. Notice how you feel in the rooms and with the people. Do you feel calm? Heard? How a place feels to you is worth noticing. If you can't be yourself, can't ask any question you want, or feel pushed into certain things, that's a red flag, and you should pay attention to it.

I toured three different places, maybe four. I wanted to feel each place's energy, and whether I would feel comfortable and at ease there. A space is just a space. One I really liked was all modern and nice, but the people there didn't make it special. My midwife's birth center wasn't the most modern space, but I felt so loved and welcomed there, and that's why I chose it.

Ask what they know about nutrition, sleep and wellbeing

Good pregnancy care is more than checkups. It includes how you eat, how you sleep and how you feel. Fueling your body is one of the most important things you can do during pregnancy, so your midwives should know a lot about it. If they can't really talk about nutrition, sleep and wellbeing, they're probably not the best fit.

What happens if I need a hospital?

Ask which hospital the center works with, how you would get there, who would come with you, and how you and the midwives would decide together when it's time to go. A good center answers this clearly and without hesitation. Read more about what a transfer usually looks like.

How long will I stay after the birth?

Ask how long families usually stay after the birth, what the midwives check on you and your baby before you go home, and whether anyone visits you at home or calls you in the days after. Every center does this a little differently, so it's worth hearing it from them.

What does it cost, and what's included?

Ask for the price in writing and what it covers: prenatal visits, the birth, postpartum visits and care for your baby. Ask whether the center works with your insurance, and how billing works if you transfer to a hospital. Here's more on what a home birth or birth center costs and checking your insurance.

Have more questions? Read the FAQ.

## Birth center vs hospital birth: the differences and the cost
URL: https://borninthenest.com/articles/birth-center-vs-hospital.html
Birth center vs hospital: who cares for you, what's available, how to find out what each costs, and questions to help you choose where to give birth.

Answers
🌷Birth center vs hospital: what's the difference?

The short answer: A birth center is all about calm, and all about you and your baby. You are the most important person in the room. You know your team, and when it's go time, your team is there for you. A hospital is a big organization, so you'll have less control over who's there and how things go. You're more likely to feel like one of many patients, and a hospital also has to run as a business. Just keep that in mind, and notice how you feel when you visit.

By Sybille Mom of two · first birth in a hospital, second at home · Education only, not medical advice

My first baby was born in a hospital. I was completely numb and felt helpless.

What I wish I'd known is that I had choices. So let's look at two of them side by side.

A note on epidurals

When labor is induced, you're usually given Pitocin, a synthetic version of oxytocin. It pushes your body into labor before it's ready, and the contractions can feel very different: stronger and unpredictable, and much harder to manage. That's how it was for me before I got the epidural. And then I felt nothing at all, which was horrible. For me, it's not an option I would ever choose again. That's why so many moms who are induced end up needing an epidural. When labor starts on its own, your body prepares itself. The contractions build step by step, and you stay in control because your body knows what it's doing. Some moms also reach for an epidural because they're in a fear state and can't get it under control. Fear can slow labor down, or make you feel like you can't cope anymore. So a lot of it is mindset, and that's something you can prepare for.

Who cares for you

At a birth center, your midwives. That's what it's all about. Get to know them, spend time with them, and see if they're the right fit for you. The right midwife makes you feel calm, heard and loved, right from the first moment. A birth center is an inviting place you get to know really well, because you go there for your visits every month, so it feels a bit like a home away from home. It's beautiful and warm. Nobody rushes you, it's calm, and there are no harsh bright lights. And just like at home, you can invite whoever you want to your birth.

At a hospital, your care is usually led by an obstetrician, a family doctor or a midwife, with nurses by your side during labor. Staff work in shifts, so you'll likely meet completely different people, and it may not be your own doctor.

What's available

At a birth center, it's not about the epidural. It's about getting you ready, over nine months, for your big marathon. You get to know your team, and they get to know you. There's no epidural or pain medication there, because when you're prepared and calm, you don't need it. Instead you can labor in a warm birth tub, move freely, and cope by understanding your body and how its natural process works.

At a hospital, epidurals, doctors and an operating room are right there. Many hospitals also offer tubs, birth balls and dimmable lights, so ask what yours has.

How birth tends to go

Wherever you give birth, at home, in a birth center or in a hospital, you can have a good birth. The difference is how your body responds to the place. In a hospital, you're often in an unfamiliar room with people you've never met. For some moms that can make the body tense up and slow labor down, and when labor slows, interventions can become more likely. For others it doesn't change a thing. At home or in a birth center, you're with a team you know, in a place you've gotten to know, which can make it easier for your body to relax and do its work.

What it costs

I paid $5,600 to my birth center midwives. A hospital birth can cost a lot more or less depending on your plan. It depends on your insurance either way, so ask your insurer and each place for their prices. Ask the center for its price and what it includes, and ask the hospital what a birth there usually costs. Here's more on insurance.

Questions to help you choose

Where do I picture myself feeling calm and cared for?
Do I want an epidural available down the hall, or do I want to try other comfort tools first?
Who would care for me, and can I meet them before labor?
At a birth center: which hospital do you work with, and how would we get there if plans change?
At a hospital: can I move around, eat, use a tub and keep the lights low?
What does my insurance cover at each?
If you can't be yourself, can't ask any question you want, or feel pushed into certain things, that's a red flag, and you should pay attention to it.

Planning a visit? Here's what to ask on a birth center tour.

Many moms also consider a third option, a home birth.

Questions moms ask

Can I get an epidural at a birth center?
No, birth centers don't offer epidurals. Before you decide you'll want one, read our note on epidurals, so you know how they work and why so many moms end up needing one. Many moms find that with nine months of preparation and a team they know, they don't need one. And if you decide you want one during labor, you can always move to a hospital.
Do birth centers have doctors?
No, birth centers don't have doctors. They have midwives. For me, that's one of the best parts. Your midwives have been with many women through birth, and they're with you from the beginning to the end, so they know you and your baby inside and out. And it's not a ten-minute visit once a month. It's a much longer, deeper relationship.
Is a birth center cheaper than a hospital?
I paid $5,600 to my birth center midwives. A hospital birth can cost a lot more or less depending on your plan. It depends on your insurance either way, so ask your insurer and each place for their prices.
Can I have a midwife at a hospital?
Yes. Many hospitals have midwives. Ask your hospital or insurance company how to find one.
Can I make a hospital birth feel calmer?
Often, yes. Ask about dimming the lights, moving around, eating and drinking, using a tub, and who can be with you. Bring your own playlist and pillow. One important thing: write down everything that matters to you before labor starts, because once it begins you won't want to talk much. You'll have so much going on. Share it with your partner, and with your midwife if you have one, so they can speak up for you.

## Does insurance cover a home birth? Medicaid and private plans
URL: https://borninthenest.com/articles/does-insurance-cover-home-birth.html
Does insurance or Medicaid cover a home birth? How it depends on your plan and your midwife, and the questions to ask.

Answers
📋Does insurance cover a home birth?

The short answer: Sometimes. It depends on your insurance plan, your state and your midwife. Some state Medicaid programs cover home births, some only with certain providers. Many midwives also offer self-pay prices, payment plans or paperwork you can send to your insurance yourself.

By Sybille Mom of two · first birth in a hospital, second at home · Education only, not medical advice

I know insurance isn't the most romantic part of planning a birth. 😄 But it's one of the most useful calls you'll make, and the earlier you make it, the more relaxed you'll feel.

Here's the honest truth: there's no single answer. Coverage depends on your midwife, your state and your plan, so let's take them one at a time.

1. Your midwife

Ask every midwife whether she works with insurance, which plans she can bill, and what a self-pay price or payment plan would look like. Many midwives will help you check your coverage, so it's a great question for your first visit.

2. Your state, if you have Medicaid

Medicaid coverage for home birth differs from state to state. Some programs cover it, some only with certain providers, and some require prior approval. Ask your state's Medicaid office.

Check your state's Medicaid program to see what its pregnancy and postpartum coverage includes. Whether it covers a particular home birth midwife is a question to ask both Medicaid and the midwife directly.

3. Your plan, if you have private insurance

Private plans vary a lot. Some pay for home birth with an in-network midwife, some pay part of it as out-of-network care, and some don't pay for it at all. Many midwives can help. For example, one midwife's practice says it bills insurance, and another lists separate pricing for a limited number of insurance plans.

The call to make

Call the number on the back of your insurance card and ask:

Do you cover a planned home birth? What about a birth center birth?
Do you cover midwife care at home or in a birth center?
Is this midwife in network? If not, how much would you pay out of network?
What would I pay for labs, ultrasounds and the newborn's care?
If my plans change and I go to the hospital, what would that cost?
Do I need prior approval for any of this?

Write down the date, the name of the person you spoke with and what they said. Many plans don't cover home birth, but it's worth a quick call to ask. Then you can focus on the exciting part: meeting your baby.

If insurance won't pay

You still have options. Many midwives offer a self-pay price, a payment plan or a sliding scale. Some accept HSA and FSA payments. Here's how to find out what a home birth costs.

Questions moms ask

Does Medicaid cover home birth?
In some states. Coverage differs from state to state, and some programs only cover certain providers. Ask your state's Medicaid office and your midwife.
Does insurance cover a birth center?
Many plans cover birth center care, but it depends on your plan and the birth center's network. Call your insurance company and ask the birth center which plans it accepts.
Will insurance cover a hospital transfer?
Hospital care is usually billed separately from a midwife's package, so ask your insurance company how they'd cover it before labor.
Can I get reimbursed after the birth?
Some plans reimburse out-of-network care after you submit the paperwork. Ask your midwife whether she provides a claim form or receipt for your insurance.
What should I ask a midwife about insurance?
Ask whether she bills insurance, which plans she works with, what her self-pay price is and whether she offers payment plans.

## How to find a home birth midwife near you
URL: https://borninthenest.com/articles/find-a-home-birth-midwife.html
How to find a home birth midwife near you: search online, read reviews, book a consultation, and notice how you feel.

Answers
🧭How do I find a home birth midwife near me?

The short answer: The internet and AI are your friends here. Search online or ask an AI assistant for midwives, birth centers and hospitals near you, and read what other moms say in their reviews. Then book a consultation with two or three, and notice how you feel with each one.

By Sybille Mom of two · first birth in a hospital, second at home · Education only, not medical advice

Finding my midwives changed everything for me. They felt a little like superheroes. They paid attention to everything: what I was eating, how I was sleeping, how I was really feeling. Often they seemed to understand what I needed just by looking at me, before I said a word.

So if you're searching for a midwife right now, I'm so excited for you. Here's how I'd start.

Step 1: Search online

The internet and AI are your friends here. Search online or ask an AI assistant for midwives, birth centers and hospitals near you, and read what other moms say in their reviews. I think those matter a lot, because real moms are sharing how it really went. Directories are a second option, but honestly they're so-so. Trust what other moms say.

Step 2: Ask around

Some of the kindest midwives aren't easy to find online. Ask friends who've had a home birth, local moms' groups, doulas, childbirth educators and birth centers. When the same name comes up again and again, that tells you something.

Step 3: Book a consultation with two or three

Most midwives offer a consultation. Bring your partner and your questions. Here's my list of questions to ask a home birth midwife.

Step 4: Notice how you feel

This part is easy to skip and so important. Pay attention to your very first feelings when you walk in, and to the people you meet and talk with. Do you feel loved, calm and heard? If you can't be yourself, can't ask any question you want, or feel pushed into certain things, that's a red flag, and you should pay attention to it. As my midwife always said, pregnant women need to feel loved. When I was pregnant, just a message from one of my midwives could calm me down and make my whole day feel lighter.

Questions moms ask

When should I start looking for a midwife?
Early in pregnancy is a good time, because popular midwives can book up for certain months. But it's rarely too late to ask. Some midwives welcome moms who switch later in pregnancy. Here's more on when to decide and how to switch.
How far away can my midwife live?
Ask her. Many midwives only serve certain counties or areas, and she'll talk with you about her travel time to your home.
Can I switch midwives during pregnancy?
Yes. If something doesn't feel right, you can look for someone else, even later in pregnancy. Just ask the new midwife what's possible.
How many midwives should I interview?
Two or three is a good start. Most offer a consultation. Compare how each one answers your questions and how you feel with her.

## Home birth or birth center for your first baby?
URL: https://borninthenest.com/articles/home-birth-or-birth-center-first-baby.html
Choosing between a home birth and a birth center for your first baby? How they're alike, how they differ, and questions to help you decide.

Answers
🏡Home birth or birth center for my first baby?

The short answer: If you love your home, and the birth center you've signed up with also does home births, wonderful. I think you should do it. Just know that birth is physical. There's some blood, and there will be some laundry. Your midwives will help clean up, but if you'd rather not have any of that in your house, choose the birth center. That's a great choice too.

By Sybille Mom of two · first birth in a hospital, second at home · Education only, not medical advice

If you're choosing between a home birth and a birth center for your first baby, I want to start with a little celebration. You already know you have choices. I didn't, with my first. 💛

If you love your home, and the birth center you've signed up with also does home births, wonderful. I think you should do it. Just know that birth is physical. There's some blood, and there will be some laundry. Your midwives will help clean up, but if you'd rather not have any of that in your house, choose the birth center. That's a great choice too. For me, it was home. I love my house, my food, my room and the way it smells, and I wanted my family around me. I didn't want to go anywhere, not even a day or two later. I just wanted to stay. But I would have been perfectly happy at the birth center too. What mattered most was that my family and my midwives were there. A home birth also means there's nothing to pack and nowhere to drive. It's one less thing to think about. And with my second baby, I already had my daughter at home. I worried that if labor started at night, my husband would have to stay home with her, or we'd have to find someone to watch her. For me, it was just easier to do it at home.

What they have in common

Both a home birth and a birth center birth are usually led by midwives. Both are built around calm, undisturbed birth, with time to get to know your midwife during pregnancy. And both are planned with a clear way to get to a hospital if you need or want more help.

If no one around you has done either, you're not alone.

At home

Your midwife comes to you. You labor in your own space, in your own bed or a birth pool, eating your own snacks, with only the people you choose. For my second birth, that meant my own bed, a steak dinner (about five minutes later it was go time 🥩) and my first child there for the first part, so proud to help her mama, until it was time for her to go to bed.

At a birth center

A birth center is an inviting place you get to know really well, because you go there for your visits every month, so it feels a bit like a home away from home. It's beautiful and warm. Nobody rushes you, it's calm, and there are no harsh bright lights. And just like at home, you can invite whoever you want to your birth. Some moms love that it feels like home without being home: no laundry, no siblings to plan around, and a place that's set up just for birth.

A few questions to help you choose

Does your birth center also offer home births? Not all of them do.
Where do I picture myself feeling most relaxed when labor gets intense?
How do I feel about leaving home during labor, or about staying put?
How far is each option from my home, and from a hospital?
Who do I want with me, and is there room for them?
What does my insurance cover for each? Here's more on insurance.
How did I feel when I met the midwives at each place?
If you can't be yourself, can't ask any question you want, or feel pushed into certain things, that's a red flag, and you should pay attention to it.

Visit a birth center if you can, and meet a home birth midwife or two. Your body will often tell you before your mind does.

Questions moms ask

Is a birth center or home birth better for a first baby?
Both are amazing choices. If you love your home and your birth center also does home births, I think you should do it. If you'd rather not have the blood and laundry in your house, the birth center is a great choice too. What matters most is that you feel calm and loved, and that your midwives and the people you love are there.
Do birth centers have birth pools?
Most do. You can labor in a warm birth tub, and many have big beds and room for your partner. Ask when you visit. And you can have one at home too. My midwives brought a birth pool to my house.
How long do families stay after a birth center birth?
Usually only a few hours, then you go home to rest. Ask each birth center how long families stay and when your follow-up visits are. With a home birth, you don't have to go anywhere at all.
How do I find a birth center near me?
The internet and AI are your friends here. Search online or ask an AI assistant for birth centers near you, and read what other moms say in their reviews. Then book a consultation with two or three, and ask whether they also offer home births. Not all of them do.
How do I tell my family?
If you feel weird about telling anyone, don't tell anyone. That's my biggest suggestion. You can simply say, "I have midwives, and I'm still looking at my options." That's it. If your family is supportive, absolutely tell them. For me, being pregnant made my anxiety higher, so I didn't want to be around negativity. If I noticed someone was skeptical of home birth, I didn't discuss it with them, and that's totally fine. And if someone starts telling you what they think about home birth, you can just say, "Thank you, but I'd rather not talk about it." If you do tell them, share the plan, not just the place. Tell them about the midwives who care for you for nine months, and how much they ask about you, like what you eat and how you sleep. It's a completely different kind of care. Many people don't know that, and they think a home birth is something you just wing. It's actually more like preparing for a marathon.

## Home birth transfer to hospital: what really happens
URL: https://borninthenest.com/articles/home-birth-transfer-to-hospital.html
What a hospital transfer during a planned home birth usually looks like: why it happens, how your midwife plans for it, and what to ask her.

Answers
🗺️What happens if you need to transfer to the hospital during a home birth?

The short answer: A transfer simply means your care moves to the hospital, because you or your baby could use more help, or because you'd like something home can't offer, like an epidural. Common reasons include a long, slow labor, being exhausted or wanting more pain relief. Your midwife plans the route with you months ahead and usually comes along.

By Sybille Mom of two · first birth in a hospital, second at home · Education only, not medical advice

"But what if something goes wrong?" It's the first question almost every mom asks when she thinks about a home birth. And it's a good one.

Here's what I've learned: feeling calm isn't only about candles and quiet. It's also about knowing someone skilled is watching, and that there's a plan. Once you know your plan, it gets much easier to stop rehearsing "what ifs" at 3 a.m. and get back to the important stuff, like sleeping and snacks.

The plan starts at your very first visit

A good home birth midwife talks about the hospital long before labor: which one, how long it takes to get there, how you'd travel, and what would make her recommend going. Choosing where to give birth includes a clear plan for getting to the hospital, if it's ever needed.

So a transfer isn't an improvised moment. It's a plan you made together, sitting on your sofa, months earlier.

What I loved was knowing how experienced my midwives were. I trusted that they would know if I needed to transfer, so I didn't have to worry about it. I could just do my thing and feel comfortable at home, and if there was a sign, I knew they'd notice right away. That was my experience with my midwives, and it's a big part of why choosing someone you trust matters so much.

Why a transfer might happen

A transfer can happen during labor or after the birth. Common reasons include a labor that's moving slowly, being exhausted, or wanting more pain relief, like an epidural.

Sometimes your midwife notices something she'd like a doctor to look at more closely. Sometimes it's after the birth, when you or your baby need a check that's easier at the hospital. And if this is your first baby, it's extra worth talking through with your midwife ahead of time.

If you ask for an epidural, that isn't giving up. That's you listening to your body, and it's a perfectly good reason to go.

What a transfer usually looks like

Every midwife does it a little differently, so ask yours. Often it looks something like this:

She tells you what she's noticing and what she recommends, so you can decide together.
She calls ahead to the hospital, so they know you're coming.
You travel by car or by ambulance, whichever your midwife recommends.
She comes with you or meets you there, and shares your notes with the hospital team.
The hospital team takes over your care. Your midwife may keep caring for you there, or stay with you as support. Ask her what that looks like.

The hospital team is there for exactly these moments, and I'm so grateful they exist.

Bring your calm with you

My first birth taught me how much it matters to feel included in what's happening. So if you ever transfer, bring your voice along. Ask what's happening and why. Ask for a minute to talk it over. Ask for your partner to stay close. Dim the lights if you can, and put your breathing music back on. Your birth is still your birth, wherever it happens.

A small "just in case" bag

ID and your insurance card
A copy of your birth preferences, with a short "if plans change" page
Phone charger and headphones
Something comfortable to wear home, for you and the baby
A car seat installed in the car (you'll need it either way)
Snacks for your partner. Trust me on this one. 🍪

Questions to ask your midwife about transfer

Which hospital would we go to, and how long does the drive take?
What would make you recommend going? Is there anything that would mean planning a hospital birth from the start?
When would we drive ourselves, and when would you call an ambulance?
Do you come with me, and will you stay?
How often do your clients transfer, especially first-time moms, and why?
What's included in your fee if we transfer, and what would be billed separately?

They know you, and they're the right people to help you plan.

Questions moms ask

Does my midwife come with me if I transfer?
Many home birth midwives travel with you or meet you at the hospital and share your notes with the team there. Ask her at your first visit whether she can keep caring for you at the hospital, or stay with you as support.
Will I have to go by ambulance?
Not always. Depending on the situation, families may travel by car with their midwife or by ambulance. Your midwife will tell you what she'd recommend and when, so it's a great thing to talk about ahead of time.
Can I still have my birth preferences at the hospital?
Yes, you can bring them and share them. Things might change depending on why you're there, but asking for dim lights, your music, your partner close by and time to make decisions is always okay.
Does a hospital transfer cost extra?
Often it does, because hospital, doctor and ambulance services are usually billed separately from a midwife's package. For example, one midwife's practice lists physician, hospital and ambulance charges as not included. Ask your midwife and your insurance company what would be covered.
Is it a failure if I transfer?
Not at all. A transfer means you and your team made a good decision together, with your baby at the center. That's exactly what a plan is for.

## Home birth with your first baby: what first-time moms ask
URL: https://borninthenest.com/articles/home-birth-with-first-baby.html
Thinking about a home birth for your first baby? What first-time moms ask, how to prepare, and the questions to take to an experienced midwife.

Answers
🌱Can I have a home birth with my first baby?

The short answer: Many first-time moms do plan a home birth. Whether it's a good fit for you depends on your own health and your own pregnancy, so the kindest first step is a conversation with an experienced midwife. A first labor often takes its time, so it helps to prepare well and to make a plan for every path.

By Sybille Mom of two · first birth in a hospital, second at home · Education only, not medical advice

I'll be honest with you from the start: my home birth was my second baby, not my first. My first baby was born in a hospital with an epidural. So I can't tell you what a first home birth feels like from my own body.

But I can tell you this. No one told me I had another option until my second pregnancy. I wish someone had, sooner. That's why I love this question so much. If you're asking it with your first baby, you're already further along than I was.

Yes, it's a real option

A planned home birth is a real option in the US. You can choose wherever you want to give birth. It's your choice. Some moms having their first baby asked the very same question you're asking now.

Whether it's right for you is a different question, and it's a personal one. It depends on your health, your pregnancy, where you live and what feels right in your heart.

What's a little different with a first baby

Everything is new the first time. Your body hasn't done this before, and you haven't either. A first labor often takes its time, so plans can change along the way, and that's okay.

That's why a good midwife will talk with you early about every path: staying home, and what would happen if you'd like or need to go to the hospital. It's also why some first-time moms love the idea of a birth center, a calm, home-like middle path. Both are good choices, and you don't have to decide on day one.

How I'd prepare, if I were you

My confidence didn't come all at once. At the start of my second pregnancy, I didn't have it yet. It grew month by month, through monthly visits with my midwives, then weekly ones near the end, books and hypnobirthing practice. By month eight, I trusted my body more than I ever had.

If I were a first-time mom thinking about home birth, I'd start in the same place:

Meet one or two midwives early. Many offer a consultation. Here are the questions I'd ask. If you don't know where to look yet, here's how to find a home birth midwife.
Learn how birth really works. A good childbirth class, a few calm books and some hypnobirthing practice can help you learn how birth really works, not the movie version. Labor comes in waves, and between contractions you get real breaks to rest and breathe. Nature doesn't want you to suffer. Your body knows how to do this. And if birth feels scary right now, you are not alone.
Bring your partner along. It's their first birth too, and they'll feel calmer if they know the plan.
Make a plan for every path. Ask your midwife what happens if you need to go to the hospital, so that part feels known instead of scary.

What should I know first?

Every mom should ask this question, and I'm so glad you're asking it. The honest answer depends on your own health and your own pregnancy, so it's different for every one of us. An experienced midwife will look at your whole picture with you and tell you honestly whether home birth is a good fit for you. For me, with my midwives, I felt cared for and loved.

They know you and your pregnancy, and they're the right people to help you decide.

Questions moms ask

What should I know about a home birth with my first baby?
It's a question every mom should ask. The honest answer depends on your own health and your own pregnancy, so it's different for every one of us. An experienced midwife will look at your whole picture with you and tell you honestly whether home birth is a good fit for you. For me, with my midwives, I felt cared for and loved.
Do midwives take first-time moms for home births?
Many do. Each midwife has her own guidelines and each state has its own rules, so ask her directly at your first consultation.
Should I choose a birth center instead for my first baby?
Some first-time moms love a birth center as a calm, home-like middle path, and some feel most relaxed at home. There's no one right answer. Visit, ask questions and notice where you feel most at ease.
When should I start planning?
Early in pregnancy works well, because you'll have time to get to know your midwife. But it's rarely too late to ask. Some midwives welcome moms who switch later in pregnancy.
Can I change my mind later?
Yes. You can change providers or plans during pregnancy, and you can ask for an epidural in labor if you want one. Choosing a plan isn't a promise you have to keep no matter what.

## How much does a home birth cost? How to find out, and what to ask
URL: https://borninthenest.com/articles/how-much-does-a-home-birth-cost.html
How to find out what a home birth costs, where midwives list their prices, what a midwife's package usually includes, what's billed separately, and the money questions to ask.

Answers
💛How much does a home birth cost?

The short answer: It depends on the midwife, your state and your insurance. Ask each midwife for her fee and what it includes, and many midwives list their prices on their own websites. Most packages cover prenatal visits, the birth and postpartum care, and hospital or doctor charges are usually billed separately.

By Sybille Mom of two · first birth in a hospital, second at home · Education only, not medical advice

Money is one of those questions many of us feel a little shy asking. Please don't be. A good midwife expects it, and she'll walk you through it kindly. Knowing the numbers early means fewer surprises later, and more room to relax and enjoy your pregnancy.

Where to start

Home birth fees vary from one midwife to the next. What you actually pay depends on your insurance, your state and the midwife you choose. The quickest way to know is to ask each midwife for her fee and what it covers, then call your insurance company.

Where to see prices

Some midwives list their prices on their own websites, so you can see them before you call. Packages differ: some are all-inclusive, some include home visits, and some offer a lower price if you pay early or flexible payments.

Prices change, so always check with the midwife directly.

What's usually included

Most packages cover the whole journey with one person you get to know: your prenatal visits, labor and birth at home, and postpartum visits for you and your baby. Some include extras like home visits, a birth pool or a book.

What's often billed separately

Every practice is different, so ask what falls outside the package. For example, one midwife's practice lists these as not included:

Physician, hospital, lab and anesthesia charges
Ambulance charges, if they're ever needed
Routine labs, billed to insurance or at a discounted cash rate
Childbirth class and doula fees

The money questions to ask

What exactly does your fee include, and what isn't included?
Do you bill insurance, or will you give me paperwork to send in myself?
Do you accept HSA or FSA payments?
Do you offer payment plans or a sliding scale?
When is the deposit due, and is any of it refundable?
What would I pay if my plans change partway through?

For me, the cost was about so much more than a birth. It was months of visits with women who paid attention to everything, and who could calm me down with a single message. That's worth asking about too.

Questions moms ask

Is a home birth cheaper than a hospital birth?
It depends on the midwife, the hospital and your insurance plan. Ask your midwife for her fee, and ask your insurance company what you'd pay for each option.
Does insurance pay for a home birth?
Sometimes. It depends on your plan, your state and your midwife. Here's more on insurance and home birth.
Can I pay for a home birth over time?
Many midwives offer payment plans. Some ask for a deposit early in pregnancy and the rest by a set week. Just ask.
Can I use my HSA or FSA?
Some midwives accept HSA and FSA payments. Check with your midwife and your plan administrator.
Why do prices vary so much?
Prices depend on where you live, what's included (like home visits or a birth pool), and the midwife's experience. Comparing what's included is as important as comparing the total.

## How to prepare your home for a home birth: a checklist
URL: https://borninthenest.com/articles/how-to-prepare-your-home-for-a-home-birth.html
How to get your home ready for a home birth: the room, the supplies, the snacks, your people and your plan, with a checklist to share.

Answers
🪺How do I prepare my home for a home birth?

The short answer: Start with your midwife's list, because every midwife has her own. Most families pick a room, protect the bed or floor, gather towels and supplies, stock up on snacks and drinks, make a plan for older children and pets, and keep the hospital route and bag ready, just in case. Then make it feel like your nest.

By Sybille Mom of two · first birth in a hospital, second at home · Education only, not medical advice

In Lesson 1, I ask where you'd feel calmest giving birth. For me, the answer was home: somewhere quiet and familiar, where no one bothers you. Preparing your home for a home birth is really just that. You're building your nest.

My second baby was born at home, in my own bed. Here's how I'd think about getting ready.

Start with your midwife's list

Every midwife has her own list, and many ask you to order a birth kit with supplies ahead of time. Ask for her list early, so you can gather things slowly instead of all at once in the last week. Here's what she'll usually bring herself.

Choose your space

Where do you picture yourself? Your bed, the living room, a birth pool, a quiet corner? Choose a main space, but don't be surprised if labor has its own ideas. Many women move around a lot.

Protect the bed or floor. Many families use a waterproof mattress cover or a plastic sheet under clean old sheets.
Gather towels. Old ones you won't miss.
Think about light and warmth. Lamps you can dim, and a warm room for when your baby arrives.
If you're using a birth pool, do a practice fill so you know how long it takes and where the hose goes.

Fuel for the marathon

At home, you eat and drink whenever you like. Snacks, tea, honey sticks, whatever your body asks for. Labor is a marathon, and you get to fuel it. 🍯 (Personal note: I had a steak dinner, and about five minutes later it was go time. Zero regrets. 🥩)

Stock up on easy snacks and drinks for you, your partner and your midwives, and freeze a few meals for the days after the birth.

Your people

Decide who you want with you: your partner, your midwives, a doula, your mom, a friend, or no one else at all. If you have older children, make a plan for them. When my second child was born, my first child was there for the first part, so proud to help her mama, until it was time for her to go to bed. 💛 Plan for pets too.

Your calm

Gather whatever helps you feel calm: your playlist, your hypnobirthing tracks, a favorite blanket, your own clothes. Hypnobirthing practice was a big part of how my confidence grew in my second pregnancy.

Your plan for every path

Part of a calm nest is knowing the plan if things change. Keep your midwife's number handy, know the route to the hospital you chose together, keep the car ready, and pack a small bag for you and your baby, just in case. Here's what happens if you need to transfer.

A checklist

Midwife's supply list and birth kit, ordered
Waterproof cover, old sheets and towels
Birth pool, practice-filled (if you're using one)
Dimmable lamps, a warm room
Snacks, drinks and a few frozen meals
Plan for older children and pets
Playlist, hypnobirthing tracks, comfy clothes
Midwife's number, hospital route and a small bag

She'll walk through your home plan with you, often at a home visit late in pregnancy.

Questions moms ask

When should I have my home ready for a home birth?
Many midwives suggest having everything ready a few weeks before your due date. Ask yours when she'd like your supplies gathered.
Do I need a special bed or room?
No. Many women give birth in their own bed or wherever they feel most comfortable. Your midwife will help you set up the space you choose.
Will a home birth make a mess?
Less than most people imagine. Midwives bring supplies, protect the bed or floor and often tidy up before they leave.
Can my older children be at the birth?
Many families include older children for part of the birth or all of it. Make a plan with someone who can care for them if they need a break.
Do I need to pack a hospital bag for a home birth?
A small bag is a kind thing to have ready, just in case your plans change. Ask your midwife what she'd put in it.

## When your partner is worried about home birth
URL: https://borninthenest.com/articles/partner-worried-about-home-birth.html
When your partner is worried about a home birth: why the worry makes sense, meeting the midwife together, hearing the transfer plan, and taking your time.

Answers
🤝My partner is worried about a home birth. What can help?

The short answer: Take the worry seriously and bring your partner into the decision. Meet the midwife together, ask her to walk you both through her transfer plan, and give it time. You don't have to settle it in one conversation.

By Sybille Mom of two · first birth in a hospital, second at home · Education only, not medical advice

If your partner is worried about a home birth, that isn't a bad sign. Often it means they care about you and the baby, and they want to know there's a plan. My first baby was born in a hospital, and no one told me I had other options until my second pregnancy. So a partner who hesitates isn't being difficult. They may simply be hearing something new.

My partner was definitely worried. For him, the hospital was the only option and everything he had ever known, and he felt I would probably get the best care there. I kept reassuring him that this was what I wanted and that it was the right path.

Then he came to every monthly visit and met the midwives, and he felt more confident in the process than ever. He saw how much care they put into me and the baby. What I saw at the hospital was different: some quick questions about the baby and an offer of vaccines, and no questions about my nutrition, my sleep or my bowel movements. That convinced him it was the right path.

What partners often worry about

Often they're the same questions you had: What if something goes wrong? Who is in charge? How quickly can we get to a hospital? What am I supposed to do? These are good questions, and a good home birth midwife expects to answer every one of them.

Meet the midwife together

Bring your partner to the consultation and let them ask their own questions, even the ones that feel awkward. Then notice how she answers: calmly, directly, without brushing anything off.

For me, it came down to a gut feeling about my midwife, and how loved and cared for she and her team made me feel. Trusting your gut is something you may have to learn again. It's a skill many of us don't practice much. Your partner deserves the chance to get their own feeling about her, too. Here's my list of questions to ask a home birth midwife.

Ask for the transfer plan, out loud

Ask your midwife to explain her plan to both of you: which hospital, how you would get there, and what would make her recommend going.

Your midwife watches closely and will tell you if it's time to go, and you make that call with her. That can be a relief for a partner, because they don't have to judge the moment alone. I trusted that my midwives would know if I needed to transfer, so I didn't have to worry about it. Read more about what happens if you need to go to the hospital and what a home birth midwife brings.

Give your partner a real role

Knowing what to do can help a partner feel calmer. Ask your midwife what she would like your partner to help with during labor and after the birth, and practice breathing and comfort ideas together during pregnancy.

During my second birth, as the contractions got stronger, a moment of fear showed up ("I'm not a marathon runner!"), and my husband said, "You totally are. You trained for this." That was all I needed.

What helped my partner most was hearing the transfer plan, and hearing the midwives talk it through. The midwives told me they attend births at homes and birth centers regularly, and they told me they don't often have a reason to send a mom to the hospital. That's it.

Give it time

You don't have to decide in one conversation. Sit on it. Take it home, breathe into it and let it settle. If something feels off, for either of you, pause, write it down and ask more questions.

Confidence can grow over a pregnancy. Mine wasn't there at the start. It grew with my visits with my midwives, my own reading and my hypnobirthing practice.

And if the two of you decide together that a birth center or a hospital fits better, that's a good outcome too. What matters is that you both feel calm about where your baby is born.

They know you and your pregnancy, and they can help you decide.

Questions moms ask

What if my partner still doesn't want a home birth?
Keep talking, and keep asking questions together. For some couples a birth center feels like a middle path. You can also ask your midwife whether your partner can bring their questions to her directly.
Should my partner come to prenatal visits?
If they can, yes. Getting to know the midwife and her team often makes the plan feel real and much less scary.
Is it normal for partners to be scared of the birth itself?
Yes. Birth is big for partners too. Talking about it openly, and knowing what their role will be, can help.

## What to ask a home birth midwife: interview questions
URL: https://borninthenest.com/articles/questions-to-ask-a-home-birth-midwife.html
The questions I'd ask a home birth midwife: how she makes you feel, her training, who comes with her, what she brings, her hospital plan, and the cost.

Answers
🫖What questions should I ask a home birth midwife?

The short answer: Notice how you feel. This is the most important one. When you take your first step into the birth center or the office, do you feel calm? Do you feel like you'd love to hang out there and just be around your midwives, without even having to talk? That's the feeling we're going for. Then you can ask all the other questions.

By Sybille Mom of two · first birth in a hospital, second at home · Education only, not medical advice

In my first pregnancy, I hardly asked anything. Fear guided my whole pregnancy, so I did what was recommended to me and kept my questions to myself. I didn't even know I could ask.

By my second pregnancy, I'd learned to ask. Big questions, small questions, and one I'd never have dared to say out loud before: what does labor actually feel like when I'm not numb? Every answer made me feel a little calmer.

So here's the list I wish I'd had the first time. You don't need to ask every question. Pick the ones that make your heart beat a little faster, and bring them to a consultation. Most midwives offer one.

Notice how you feel

This is the most important one. When you take your first step into the birth center or the office, do you feel calm? Do you feel like you'd love to hang out there and just be around your midwives, without even having to talk? That's the feeling we're going for. Then you can ask all the other questions. If you can't be yourself, can't ask any question you want, or feel pushed into certain things, that's a red flag, and you should pay attention to it.

Ask what they know about nutrition, sleep and wellbeing

Good pregnancy care is more than checkups. It includes how you eat, how you sleep and how you feel. Fueling your body is one of the most important things you can do during pregnancy, so your midwives should know a lot about it. If they can't really talk about nutrition, sleep and wellbeing, they're probably not the best fit.

Her training and experience

How many births have you attended as the lead midwife?
Are you trained in newborn resuscitation, and how do you keep your skills fresh?
Could I talk to a couple of families you've cared for?

Who comes with her

Who else comes to the birth: a second midwife, an assistant?
Who's your backup if you're sick, or at another birth that night?
Can I meet everyone before labor? (New faces are fine, just maybe not in the middle of a contraction.)

When I asked my midwives whether I needed a doula, they smiled and said, "We are your doula." Ask yours, and listen to how she answers.

Your pregnancy care

How often will we meet, where, and for how long?
Who orders my lab work and ultrasounds?
How do you prepare women for birth? Are there classes you recommend?
How can I reach you between visits, and how quickly do you usually reply?

Labor and birth

When do you come to me once labor starts?
How do you listen to my baby and check on me during labor?
Can I eat, drink, move and use a birth pool? (I had a steak dinner, and about five minutes later it was go time. Zero regrets. 🥩)
What comfort tools do you use?
How will my partner be part of it, and older children if I'd like them there?

What she brings

What equipment and medicines do you bring to a home birth?

She typically brings a handheld device to listen to your baby's heartbeat, a blood pressure cuff, oxygen, equipment to help a baby breathe if needed and medicine to help with bleeding. What's included depends on her training, so it's a great thing to ask about.

If plans change

Which hospital would we go to, and how long does it take to get there?
What would make you recommend seeing a doctor during pregnancy, or going to the hospital in labor?
Do you come with me if we transfer, and do you send my notes ahead?
How often do the first-time moms you care for end up transferring, and why?

That last one can feel awkward to ask. Ask anyway. There's no "right" number. What you're listening for is how calmly and clearly she explains it.

After the birth

How many postpartum visits do you make, and where?
What newborn checks and screenings do you offer?
Who helps with breastfeeding?
Who do I call at 2 a.m. in the first week? (There will be a 2 a.m. call.)

The money questions

What's your total fee, and what's included?
What's not included? Lab work, ultrasounds, a birth pool, hospital or ambulance costs if we transfer?
Do you bill insurance or give me what I need to ask for reimbursement? Can I use my HSA or FSA?
Do you offer payment plans?

Every practice packages things differently. For example, one midwife's practice lists hospital, lab and ambulance charges as not included in its package, so it really pays to ask.

After the call

After the call, sit quietly for a minute and notice how you feel. Calm? Heard? A little bit loved? My midwives felt like superheroes to me. They paid attention to everything, and often understood what I needed before I said a word. As my midwife always said, pregnant women need to feel loved. If your gut says yes, that matters.

And one last question for her: Do I have to decide right now? A good midwife will smile and give you time.

Questions moms ask

How many midwives should I interview?
Two or three is a good start. Most midwives offer a consultation, so you can compare how each one answers your questions and how you feel with her.
When should I start looking for a home birth midwife?
Many women start looking early in pregnancy, but it's rarely too late to ask. Some practices welcome women who switch later in pregnancy, so just call and ask what's possible.
Is it rude to ask a midwife how often her clients transfer?
Not at all. It's one of the kindest questions you can ask, for both of you. A good midwife expects it and will tell you how often her clients transfer, the usual reasons, and how she handles it.
What if I don't like the answers?
Then you've learned something important, and that's a good thing. Keep looking until you find someone who makes you feel calm, heard and cared for.

Keep reading

## How to tell your family you're planning a home birth
URL: https://borninthenest.com/articles/telling-family-about-home-birth.html
Telling family about a home birth: why it's okay to wait until after, what to share if you do, answering a worried reaction, and older children at the birth.

Answers
💬How do I tell my family I'm planning a home birth?

The short answer: You don't have to tell anyone before the birth. I didn't, and that was okay. If you do share, tell them about the plan, not just the place: who your midwife is and that she has a transfer plan with a hospital. Listen to their worry, and remember you don't owe anyone a debate.

By Sybille Mom of two · first birth in a hospital, second at home · Education only, not medical advice

Telling your family can feel harder than making the decision. Here's what I did: I didn't tell anybody about my home birth until after the fact.

It's okay not to tell anyone until after

I didn't want the worry on me. In my experience, if your friends or family probably won't support it, mentioning it doesn't help. They may just worry, and that worry can pull you into a negative space. So I told nobody until after the birth, and it was wonderful.

That's what felt right for me. It's okay if it feels right for you too, and it's also okay to share. You don't owe anyone your birth plans. Pregnancy brings many decisions, and you don't have to make them in the moment. Sit on it, and share when you're ready, whether that's early, after you've met your midwife, or after your baby is here.

Telling people after the birth

If you wait, you get to share the news in your own words, with your baby already in your arms.

The reactions were crazy. People were worried at first, but then I told them the story, and they couldn't believe how amazing it was. They also couldn't believe that I just stayed in my own bed after I gave birth and ate my own food, and that my midwives came the next morning to check on me, instead of me having to put the baby in the car and go to a doctor. Everything happened in my house, which was the best part.

If you do tell them: share the plan, not just the place

"Home birth" on its own can sound like "no plan." What often helps is describing the care around it: who your midwife is, how often you see her, what she brings to the birth, and that she has a plan with a nearby hospital in case you need to go.

If they want to read more, you can point them to what happens if you need to go to the hospital, what a midwife brings or the birth options guide.

When someone reacts with fear

Some people have never known anyone who planned a home birth, so the first reaction might be surprise or fear. That reaction often comes from what they know, not from anything about you.

Listen first. Then answer the question underneath, which is often some version of "what if something goes wrong?" You can explain that your midwife watches closely, that she will tell you if it's time to go and you make that call with her, and that hospitals are there when more help is needed.

You can also set a boundary. It's your pregnancy and your birth. It's okay to tell people kindly that you've made your choice with your midwife and that what you need from them now is support, not a debate.

Protect your calm

Feeling calm matters in labor. Stress hormones are your body's way of protecting you. In nature, they would slow labor down if there was danger nearby. So lean on the people who make you feel loved and cared for, and give yourself permission to keep some conversations short, or to skip them for now.

If a worried relative has also scared you, write the worry down and bring it to your next visit. Your midwife can answer it for you, and you don't have to carry it alone. That's what I did, and they always had a good answer to ease my worries.

Will older children be at the birth?

Some families want older children at home during the birth. Others arrange for someone to look after them, at home or somewhere else. There's no single right answer.

If your children will be at home, it helps to have one trusted adult whose only job is to look after them, so your partner can stay with you.

At my home birth, my older child was there until bedtime. I wanted her there so she could see how amazing a birth is and that it's nothing to be afraid of. I wanted it to empower her. It's a very personal decision, but I'd encourage every mom to have her children there if they want to be, and to explain beforehand what the birth will look like. I told my child that mommy would do a lot of breathing, be very quiet and sometimes really loud.

I brought her to every checkup, and the midwives even let her check the baby's heartbeat. They involved her in every step, which I think is the best thing. She truly wanted to be there, until it was time to sleep.

Questions moms ask

Do I have to tell my family I'm planning a home birth?
No. I didn't tell anyone until after the birth, and for me that was okay. It's your choice whether, when and how much to share.
What if my family is against home birth?
Listen to their worry, tell them about the plan and the transfer arrangements, and, if you're comfortable, invite them to bring their questions to your midwife. Then let it rest. You don't have to win the conversation.
Can older children be at a home birth?
Absolutely. It's your choice. I wanted mine to be there. If they will be there, plan for a trusted adult to look after them.

## What does a home birth midwife bring?
URL: https://borninthenest.com/articles/what-does-a-home-birth-midwife-bring.html
What a home birth midwife usually brings to your birth: the equipment, the supplies, the second midwife, and the questions to ask about her kit.

Answers
🧺What does a home birth midwife bring?

The short answer: Midwives come prepared. She typically brings a handheld device to listen to your baby's heartbeat, a blood pressure cuff, oxygen, equipment to help a baby breathe if needed, medicine to help with bleeding, and supplies for you and your newborn. Many also bring a birth pool. What's included depends on her training and your state's rules, so ask.

By Sybille Mom of two · first birth in a hospital, second at home · Education only, not medical advice

When I tell people I had my second baby at home, one of the first questions is: "But what did the midwife actually bring?" I love that question. A lot of us imagine a midwife arriving with a towel and good intentions. 😄

Midwives come prepared. Here's what a home birth midwife usually brings, and what you might gather yourself.

What she brings

She typically brings:

A handheld device to listen to your baby's heartbeat during labor
A blood pressure cuff and other tools to check on you
Oxygen
Equipment to help a baby breathe if needed
Medicine to help with bleeding
Supplies for you and your newborn, like gloves, pads and newborn care items

What's included depends on her training. So it's a great thing to ask her.

Comfort things

Many midwives also bring, rent or recommend comfort tools, like a birth pool, a birth stool or a birth ball.

A second pair of hands

Usually, she doesn't come alone. Many home birth midwives bring a second trained midwife or assistant. Ask yours who comes with her, and when.

What you'll gather yourself

Most midwives give you a list of things to have ready at home, and some ask you to order a birth kit ahead of time. Here's how I'd prepare your home.

What I remember most

Honestly? Not the equipment. I remember how my midwives paid attention to everything. Often they seemed to understand what I needed just by looking at me, before I said a word.

Ask your midwife what she brings to your birth. Most midwives are happy to walk you through it. Ask if she can set up a birth pool in your home, too. Mine brought an inflatable pool, and I thought it was so cool.

Questions moms ask

Does a home birth midwife bring oxygen?
Many do. Ask your midwife exactly what equipment she brings and what she's trained to use.
Does the midwife bring a birth pool?
Some bring one, some rent one to you and some ask you to buy your own. Ask early so you have time to set it up and practice filling it.
What medicines can a home birth midwife carry?
Ask her what she carries and when she'd use it.
Do I need to buy a birth kit?
Many midwives ask you to order a birth kit with supplies like pads, gloves and underpads. She'll tell you what to get and when.
Will she bring an assistant?
Often, yes. Many midwives bring a second midwife or a trained assistant to the birth. Ask who it will be and whether you can meet her first.

## When to decide where to give birth, and can you switch?
URL: https://borninthenest.com/articles/when-to-decide-where-to-give-birth.html
When to decide between a home birth, a birth center or a hospital, whether it's too late to switch to a midwife, and how to change providers during pregnancy.

Answers
🗓️When do I need to decide where to give birth? Can I switch?

The short answer: Starting early gives you the most choice, because some midwives and birth centers book up. But it's rarely too late to ask. You can switch providers during pregnancy, and some midwives welcome moms who come to them later. Call, ask what's possible, and trust your gut.

By Sybille Mom of two · first birth in a hospital, second at home · Education only, not medical advice

Before my first baby, no one asked me the most important question: where do you want to give birth? I didn't even know it was a choice. No one told me I had other options until my second pregnancy. So if you're reading this in the middle of your pregnancy and wondering whether you've missed your chance, you probably haven't.

When should I start looking?

I didn't start looking for my midwife until after my first trimester, and when I met her I just had that gut feeling she was the right one.

Starting early in pregnancy gives you the most options, because popular midwives and birth centers can book up for certain months. But early isn't a deadline. If you're further along, call and ask what's possible. Here's how to find a home birth midwife.

Can I switch to a midwife later in pregnancy?

Often, yes. Some midwives welcome moms who switch later in pregnancy. Each midwife and birth center has its own rules about when they can still take someone new, and your health and your pregnancy matter too, so ask directly.

If you switch, ask your current provider for a copy of your records, so your new midwife has your full history from the start.

Can I switch from a midwife to a hospital, or back?

Yes. Plans can change, and that's okay. Sometimes it's because of your health or your baby's. Sometimes you simply feel differently than you did a few months ago. You can choose wherever you want to give birth. It's your choice. Here's how a birth center compares with a hospital.

How do I know it's time to change?

Notice how you feel after your visits. Do you feel heard? Calm? Would you keep visiting her like a friend? If something feels off, even if you can't put it into words yet, pause, write it down and ask questions. We live in a modern world with ancient instincts, so listen to yours.

My second pregnancy is when I found my midwife, and I just trusted my gut. She and her team made me feel so loved and cared for. Trusting your gut is something you may have to learn again. It's a skill many of us don't practice much.

You don't have to decide everything at once

You can choose who cares for you first and keep learning about the rest. You don't have to decide in the moment. Sit on it, breathe into it and let it settle. My own confidence wasn't there at the start. It grew over my pregnancy, with my midwives, my own reading and hypnobirthing.

If you're weighing a birth center, here's what to ask on a birth center tour. And if this is your first baby, the first-time mom guide covers the choices no one mentions.

They know you and your pregnancy, and they can help you decide.

Questions moms ask

Is it too late to switch to a midwife near the end of pregnancy?
It's rarely too late to ask. Some midwives can still take you late in pregnancy and some can't, so call and ask what's possible for you.
Do I have to decide where to give birth before my first prenatal visit?
No. You can start care, ask questions and decide as you learn. Starting the search early simply gives you more choice.
Can I change my mind after choosing a birth center or a home birth?
Yes. It's your pregnancy and your birth. Talk with your midwife or doctor about what changing would look like.
