## Your birth options in the US: home, birth center or hospital
URL: https://borninthenest.com/guides/birth-options-home-birth-center-hospital.html
An honest guide to where you can give birth in the US: home birth with a midwife, a birth center, or a hospital, and how to choose what feels right.

Guide
🏡Your birth options in the US: home, birth center or hospital
Three places, three kinds of care, and one question to help you choose.

Before my first birth, no one ever asked me where I wanted to give birth. I didn't even know it was a choice. Here's what I wish someone had told me: in the US you can plan to give birth at home, in a birth center or in a hospital, and you have the right to choose.

🏡 Home birth

At a planned home birth, a midwife cares for you through pregnancy, comes to you when labor begins, and stays with you through the birth and the first hours after. Prenatal visits are often long and unhurried, sometimes in your own living room. In labor you can move, eat, rest, use a birth pool and be surrounded only by the people you choose.

Midwives bring equipment to listen to your baby, check your blood pressure, help with bleeding and help a baby breathe if needed, and they plan a route to a hospital from the very first visit. After the birth, your midwives come back to check on you and your baby the next day, right in your own bed. They come to your house, which is amazing. Of course you can have a home birth with your first baby. Many first-time moms do, and your midwives have cared for many, many first-time moms before you.

🌿 Birth center

A birth center is an inviting place, and one you get to know really well, because you go there for your visits every month. So it feels a bit like a home away from home. That's what I love about birth centers. They're beautiful and warm. Nobody rushes you, it's calm, and there are no harsh bright lights. And just like at home, you can invite whoever you want to your birth.

🏥 Hospital

Hospitals are also an okay place to give birth, and they're a wonderful option if something doesn't go as planned. Many offer midwife care, and you can still bring calm with you, like dim lights and your own music. There are more rules and restrictions, and it's not what I would choose for myself, but if a hospital is where you feel most relaxed, that's wonderful.

How to choose

Picture your birth. Close your eyes and imagine it. Who's there? What room are you in? How does it make you feel?
Talk to different people and visit different places. Talk to midwives and doctors, visit a birth center and visit a hospital, and ask moms who have given birth in different places. The internet and AI are your friends here. Search online or ask an AI assistant for midwives and birth centers near you, and read their reviews. Everywhere you go, ask yourself: do I feel calm and loved here? If you do, wonderful, then that's a great place for you. If you can't be yourself, can't ask any question you want, or feel pushed into certain things, that's a red flag, and you should pay attention to it.
Choose your team, and take your time. When you find the midwives or doctors who make you feel calm and loved, that's your team. You wouldn't run a marathon without knowing your team, and birth is the same: you want people who know you and your baby inside and out. There's no rush. You can even start with a hospital and switch later if it doesn't feel right.

Your first steps

Find a midwife, birth center or hospital. The internet and AI are your friends here. Search online or ask an AI assistant for midwives, birth centers and hospitals near you, and read what other moms say in their reviews.
Book a consultation with two or three. Most offer one.
Notice how you feel. Pay attention to your very first feelings when you walk in, and to the people you meet and talk with. Do you feel loved, calm and heard? If you can't be yourself, can't ask any question you want, or feel pushed into certain things, that's a red flag, and you should pay attention to it.
Ask your questions about training, backup, transfer plan, equipment, cost, and what they know about nutrition, sleep and wellbeing.

Want more answers? Read the FAQ, or start with my five short lessons.

With love from my nest to yours,Sybille 🤍

## First-time mom? What no one tells you about birth choices
URL: https://borninthenest.com/guides/first-time-mom-birth-choices.html
Pregnant with your first baby? The birth choices no one mentions: where to give birth, choosing and switching providers, midwives, birth centers and what to ask.

Guide
🌱First-time mom? What no one tells you about your birth choices
The things I wish I'd known before my first baby.

My first baby was born in a hospital, the way most of us are told it should go. I was induced early and had an epidural. I was completely numb, and I felt helpless. No one ever asked me the most important question: where do you want to give birth? I didn't even know it was a choice. No one told me I had other options until my second pregnancy. I want you to know sooner.

1. You get to choose where you give birth

In the US, you have many options: you can plan a birth at home with a midwife, in a birth center or in a hospital. You can choose wherever you want to give birth. It's your choice. Read the overview of your birth options.

2. Your feelings matter to your body

When you feel calm and loved, your body can relax and let labor flow. That's why choosing where to give birth isn't only a medical question. It's also about where you feel most at ease, so your body can do what it was made to do.

3. Midwives aren't only for home births

Yes, you can have a midwife at home, in a birth center or in a hospital. Many families never meet a midwife simply because no one suggested it.

4. A birth center can be a beautiful choice for a first baby

A birth center is a home-like, midwife-led space with comfy beds and birth tubs, and for many first-time moms it feels like a calm middle path between home and hospital. Every pregnancy is different.

5. First labors are often longer, and that's okay

A long first labor doesn't mean you have to go to a hospital. It means it's even more important to find a place where you feel calm and loved. When you don't feel that way, labor can slow down or even stop, and that's when things can get complicated.

6. You can change your mind, even later in pregnancy.

The first doctor or midwife you see doesn't have to be the one who's with you at your birth. If something doesn't feel right, you can switch, even later in your pregnancy. It's your pregnancy and your birth.

Wondering if it's too late to change? Read when to decide where to give birth, and how to switch.

7. You don't have to figure it out alone

Born in the Nest has five short lessons you can read right here, and a weekly letter every Sunday, matched to your due month, all the way to the day you meet your baby. You can also read the FAQ for quick answers.

With love from my nest to yours,Sybille 🤍

## Scared of giving birth? You are not alone · Born in the Nest
URL: https://borninthenest.com/guides/scared-of-giving-birth.html
Afraid of giving birth? You're not alone. Where fear of childbirth comes from, why calm matters to your body, and things that really help.

Guide
🤍Scared of giving birth? You are not alone
Fear of birth is so common because we grew up believing birth is scary. It is not.

If you're scared of giving birth, I want you to hear this first: there is nothing wrong with you. Most of us feel some worry about birth, and many women feel real fear. You are in very good company.

Where the fear comes from

I know this fear personally. I was so excited to meet my first baby, and so scared to give birth. That fear guided my whole first pregnancy.

Fear of birth is so common because most of us grew up believing birth is scary. We've been shown the movie version: screaming, rushing, panic. But real birth doesn't look like that. Real birth happens in a quiet, calm, loving place. Just look at other mammals: if you've ever watched a dog or a cat give birth, she picks the quietest room, settles in and does her thing. Labor comes in waves, and between contractions you get real breaks to rest and breathe. Yes, there's intensity, and there can be pain, but pain and suffering aren't the same thing. Nature doesn't want you to suffer. Your body is amazing, and it knows how to do this.

For me, the difference was preparation. My midwives helped me get ready all through my pregnancy, almost like training for a big race, so I didn't walk into labor cold.

Why feeling calm matters to your body

Labor is guided by hormones. Oxytocin, often called the love hormone, powers contractions, and endorphins are your body's own comfort. They flow best when you feel calm, private and undisturbed. When you feel afraid or rushed, stress hormones like adrenaline rise, and they can slow labor down.

Stress hormones aren't bad in themselves. They're your body's way of protecting you. In nature, if there was danger nearby, they would slow labor down for a little while so a mother could move somewhere safe, and then labor would start again. But we don't live in those times anymore, so most of the time that pause isn't needed. Still, your body reacts the same way. I felt it in the hospital every time a new nurse showed up to tell me something, take my blood or run another check.

When you're scared, your body tenses up, and that makes labor harder. When you feel calm and cared for, your body can relax and do its work.

What helps

Learning how birth really works, not the movie version. Labor comes in waves, with real breaks between contractions. Nature doesn't want you to suffer.
Knowing your options. You can choose where you give birth and who is with you. Read about your birth options.
A midwife or doctor who knows you. You see the same person, or the same small team, through pregnancy and birth, so you know each other before labor.
Practicing calm breathing. Slow breaths, longer on the out-breath, practiced for weeks before so your body knows them. I practiced every time I stopped at a red traffic light while driving, and I still do.
Warm water. A bath or birth pool in labor is one comfort option many midwives and birth centers offer.
Your people. Surround yourself with those who make you feel loved. As my midwife always said, pregnant women need to feel loved.

If you're thinking about an epidural, I wrote a note on epidurals about how they often come into the picture, and why preparation matters.

Confidence can grow, little by little

I didn't feel confident at the start either. My confidence grew month by month, through regular visits with my midwives (monthly at first, then weekly near the end), books and hypnobirthing practice. By month eight, I trusted my body more than I ever had. Confident doesn't mean fearless, though. While I was giving birth to my second child and the contractions got stronger, a moment of fear showed up, and I blurted out, "I'm not a marathon runner!" My husband said, "You totally are. You trained for this." That was all I needed.

You deserve to feel supported, not judged. If you'd like a companion along the way, my five short lessons are a good place to start.

With love from my nest to yours,Sybille 🤍

## Where would you feel calmest giving birth?
URL: https://borninthenest.com/lessons/day-1.html
One question to start with, and what my own answer looked like.

Lesson 1 of 5 · Home birth, explained by a mom who's done it
🪺Where would you feel calmest giving birth?
One question to start with, and what my own answer looked like.

Home birth, explained by a mom who's done it. That's what these five short lessons are, right here on the site, no signup needed.

Fear of birth is so common because we grew up believing birth is scary. It is not. We've been shown a movie version of birth, but labor really comes in waves, with real breaks to rest and breathe. Nature doesn't want you to suffer. Your body is amazing, and it knows how to do this. Yes, there's intensity, and there can be pain. But pain and suffering aren't the same thing. Birth can be one of the most beautiful, powerful things you'll ever do. We've just been taught to see it through the wrong lens.

I'm Sybille, a mom of two. My first baby was born in a hospital with an epidural. I was completely numb, and I felt helpless. My second was born at home, in my own bed, with a midwife I trusted, and that birth showed me how calm and beautiful giving birth can be. Same body, completely different birth. The biggest difference was where I was and how calm and loved I felt.

As my midwife always said, pregnant women need to feel loved. That's what Born in the Nest is about.

Some moms love going to the hospital, and that's wonderful. But many of us don't even realize we can give birth in a place where we feel calm and loved, because our bodies already know how to do it. Women have been doing this for centuries.

So let's start with one question.

Close your eyes for a moment. Where would you feel calmest, most at ease, and most loved?

There's no wrong answer. For many of us, it's home, because home is your comfort place. It's where you spend every day, with your most trusted people, your food, your bed and all your creature comforts.

My answer, the second time. The second time, I chose home, and it wasn't only because of the lights. It was the whole environment: my own food, my family, my kids, my dog. Everybody I love was there, and that's what I loved most. And of course I know my house inside and out, so I knew which room was the quietest. For me, that was the small bathroom. At home, I could dim the lights. I had mood lighting and my own essential oils. When labor got going, I wanted darkness, and I stayed there until it was pushing time and I wanted to lie down.

With my first baby, in the hospital, they were constantly checking on me. I had what felt like a gazillion cables and monitors on me, and I hated all of that. And of course there were the bright lights. It's not a criticism of the hospital, it just wasn't for me. It wasn't the quiet nook a woman needs to give birth.

Getting ready for it. Getting ready is like preparing for a marathon: you assemble your team ahead of time, so when it's go time, you know everybody, and you trust them with everything. My midwives prepared me through my whole pregnancy. For months, I practiced breathing through each wave. So when labor came, I met it with a different mindset. For me, it was pain, but not suffering.

So when you think about where to give birth, it's not only a medical question. It's also where you'd feel calmest, and who you'd want next to you. That's a good conversation to start with your midwife or doctor.

A tiny practice for today: close your eyes and picture your birth. Who's there with you? What room are you in? And how does it make you feel? Do you feel calm, safe and relaxed? Is it even a little fun? That's the feeling we're going for.

All five lessons

Five short lessons in all. No pressure, no judgment, just what I wish someone had told me before my first birth.

Day 1Where would you feel calmest giving birth?›Day 2What birth looks like when no one's in a hurry›Day 3My two births, and what changed›Day 4My midwives saw what I needed before I said a word›Day 5The question no one asked me before my first birth›

And this isn't a one-time thing. If you'd like, I'll also send you one short letter every Sunday, matched to your due month: one honest moment, one calm idea and one small step for wherever you are. I'll also help with the practical side: how to find and choose a midwife or birth center, and the questions I had when I first decided to switch, answered one by one. These are big decisions, and I wish I'd had someone I could count on when I made them. When I was pregnant, just a message from one of my midwives could calm me down and make my whole day feel lighter. That's what I want Born in the Nest to be for you: a place you can come back to whenever you need it, every week, all the way to the day you meet your baby.

With love from my nest to yours,Sybille 🤍

## What birth looks like when no one's in a hurry
URL: https://borninthenest.com/lessons/day-2.html
Lesson 2 of 5 from Born in the Nest: Dim lights, warm water, a midwife who knows your name.

Lesson 2 of 5 · Home birth, explained by a mom who's done it
🌿What birth looks like when no one's in a hurry
Dim lights, warm water, a midwife who knows your name.

When most of us picture birth, we picture the movie version: rushing, screaming, bright lights. Real labor comes in waves, and it builds up slowly. Your body first gives you a few contractions so you can get used to them. It doesn't all hit you at once. Between contractions you get real breaks to rest and breathe. Nature doesn't want you to suffer. And when you give birth at home, with a midwife you know, nobody is in a hurry. Here's what it can look like.

Months before: you'll have regular prenatal visits with your midwife, often an hour long, sometimes in your own living room. You'll talk about nutrition, how you're feeling, your fears, and your hopes. She checks your blood pressure, measures your belly, and listens to your baby's heartbeat. By the time labor starts, she isn't a stranger. She's someone you trust.

When labor begins: you stay home, in your own clothes, eating and drinking when you want, walking around, resting in your bed. You call your midwife, and she comes when it's time. My midwife told me she always started baking something when labor began. So when your labor starts, bake something, or do whatever feels most fun and calms your mind. I cleaned up the kitchen after dinner and just walked around, because that's what I usually like to do. You can do anything you want, because you're in your own home.

Fuel for the marathon. At home, you eat and drink whenever you like. Snacks, tea, honey sticks, whatever your body asks for. Labor is a marathon, and you get to fuel it. 🍯 Wherever you give birth, ask ahead what you'll be allowed to eat and drink during labor.

(Personal note: I had a steak dinner, and about five minutes later it was go time. Zero regrets. 🥩)

Who's there: At home, you get to choose who shares this moment with you: your partner, a doula, your mom, a friend, your own children, even your dog, or no one else at all.

(When my second child was born, my first child was there for the first part, so proud to help her mama, until it was time for her to go to bed. 💛)

What she brings: midwives come prepared. She typically brings a handheld device to listen to baby's heartbeat, a blood pressure cuff, oxygen, equipment to help a baby breathe if needed, medicine to help with bleeding, and supplies for you and your newborn. (What's included depends on her training, so it's a great thing to ask her.)

What it feels like: It feels calm, relaxing and quiet, with soft lights and maybe a birth pool. Your midwife watches closely but calmly, often from the corner of the room, checking in without interrupting. There's zero stress and zero rush.

My own dark little nest: At home, you can dim the lights, bring your own scents and choose the room that feels right. You already know from Lesson 1 which room I picked: the smallest bathroom in the house, in the dark. 🌙

After the birth: this is the golden hour, and it's the most beautiful part. No checkups right away, just you and your baby. Your midwives wait until the cord stops pulsing before it's cut. Your partner is right there with you. Nothing is rushed. It's peaceful, and you get to be in your own bed, eat your own food, whatever you want.

In a hospital, after the birth is very different. Because they're a big system with a lot of liability, they have to keep running checks on you right after you give birth. They might wake you for a blood test or press on your belly. It's not something they do on purpose, it's just how a big hospital has to work. But it means that quiet, relaxing time after birth is hard to find there.

Why home can feel so different

A hospital is built to care for many people at once, with kind, hardworking teams who often work in shifts, so the person who greets you may not be the one who catches your baby. That's simply how a big, busy place works, and it's wonderful that it's there. And because a hospital is a big system, liability is a big reason they have to run so many tests and keep you on constant monitoring. That's a big part of why it feels so different from home.

When labor really gets going, your body goes inward. You can't make decisions, and you often can't even talk. So if someone asks you a bunch of questions, you can't answer them. And your partner may not know what you want either, because they've never given birth. That's why it matters so much to talk everything through with your midwives before labor starts. They'll know exactly what you want and can speak up for you when you can't. If you're giving birth in a hospital, having your own midwife there with you is wonderful for the same reason.

At home or in a birth center, the care is built around one family: yours. Your midwife doesn't need to ask you a bunch of questions, because she knows you. She's known you for the past nine months. That makes everything so much calmer. She watches closely, but she lets labor unfold at its own pace. And the only people in the room are the ones you choose, the ones who love and support you: your partner, your mom, a dear friend, maybe even your older children.

Your body was made for this. Women have given birth for thousands of years, but many of us have lost touch with that knowing, so we have to learn to tune in again. A good midwife can help you find your way back, and you can practice it yourself. And your baby takes part too. With my second birth, I felt like my baby was guiding me the whole way and taught me so much.

And if plans change? A good midwife has a transfer plan from the very first visit: which hospital, how long it takes, and when she'd recommend going. We'll talk about that on Day 4, because feeling calm also means knowing there's a backup.

With love,Sybille 🤍

## My two births, and what changed · Born in the Nest
URL: https://borninthenest.com/lessons/day-3.html
Lesson 3 of 5 from Born in the Nest: One in a hospital, one at home. Here's what I learned.

Lesson 3 of 5 · Home birth, explained by a mom who's done it
💛My two births, and what changed
One in a hospital, one at home. Here's what I learned.

Today I want to share something personal: my two births. Every birth is different, and mine isn't a rulebook. But stories have a way of making things feel possible.

My first baby: the hospital

With my first baby, I was scared. I thought I had to give birth in a hospital, and I had no idea what to expect. My labor lasted nearly two and a half days. Along the way I felt miserable and lost, because I had no control over what my body wanted to do. And after I gave birth, I was drained, but they still wouldn't feed me, and they kept asking me questions instead of letting me rest.

My second baby: at home

My second birth was a completely different story. I found the most amazing midwives, and that changed everything. I felt truly loved and cared for by these women, and they made me feel so confident that my body was ready to do this. I read a couple of books, practiced hypnobirthing, and met with them every month. Their words, their calm and their expertise prepared me for my home birth, and it became the most beautiful thing I could ever imagine.

On the day, I felt so calm and in control. It was so manageable that I told my midwife she didn't need to come over yet. Thankfully, she came anyway. At 8:30 she and another midwife were at my house, and an hour later my baby was here. It felt like five minutes.

My contractions got stronger, and I moved between sitting and standing. Then the urge to push started, and I just let my body do it. You always get a break in between. The ring of fire was real, but it lasted only a few seconds. I breathed through it, and it didn't even matter, because seconds later my baby arrived. Her eyes were so wide open, looking around the room, so awake and so beautiful.

I held her in my arms and nursed her, and we waited until the cord stopped pulsing before it was cut. It felt so amazing. There was no rushing. Then I ate a massive meal and a banana, because I was really hungry. And then I got to sleep in my own bed, in my own house, with my own family. This was the golden hour I never got at the hospital. It was the most beautiful time of my life, and that's why I started Born in the Nest: so you can experience it too.

If you asked me today, "Do you want to give birth right now?" I'd say, "Yeah, sure." It was that manageable for me, because I felt so prepared. That's what I want for you too.

What I'd tell my first-time self

If something feels off, even if you can't put it into words yet, pause. Write it down. Ask questions. There's almost always another way. We live in a modern world with ancient instincts, so listen to yours. ❤️

I'm sharing this not to say a hospital is wrong. For some women and some pregnancies, it's exactly the right place, and I'm grateful it exists. I'm sharing it because no one told me I had another option until my second pregnancy. I want you to know sooner.

More stories are coming. In the weekly Born in the Nest letter, I'll share calm, real stories from other mothers: home births, birth center births, and births where plans changed and still felt good. Stories that help you feel braver.

Have a story to share? If you've given birth at home or in a birth center and would like to help another mom feel braver, just write to me at hello@borninthenest.com. I'll always ask your permission before sharing anything, and I can keep your name private.

With love,Sybille 🤍

## My midwives saw what I needed before I said a word
URL: https://borninthenest.com/lessons/day-4.html
Lesson 4 of 5 from Born in the Nest: How midwives watch over you, and how to find comfort without an epidural.

Lesson 4 of 5 · Home birth, explained by a mom who's done it
🌬️My midwives saw what I needed before I said a word
How midwives watch over you, and how to find comfort without an epidural.

My midwives felt a little like superheroes to me. They paid attention to everything: what I was eating, how I was sleeping, how I was really feeling, and the small things I'd never have thought to mention. Often they seemed to understand what I needed just by looking at me, before I said a word. That quiet attention was the most powerful thing I experienced, and it's a big part of how midwives care for you.

When I asked my midwives whether I needed a doula, they smiled and said, "We are your doula." They were with me the whole way, not coming and going on shifts.

Because the question every mom asks is "But what if something goes wrong?" And it's a good one. Feeling calm isn't only about candles and quiet. It's also about knowing someone skilled is watching, and that there's a plan.

How midwives keep watch

Your midwife listens to your baby's heartbeat regularly throughout labor, checks your blood pressure, pulse, and temperature, and watches how labor is progressing. She's trained to notice early signs that something needs more help, often long before it becomes urgent.

When a home birth might still be possible.

Ask before you rule it out. That's my biggest wish for you here.

In my first pregnancy, I was told at the hospital that I had high blood pressure. It turned out to be nerves: hospitals just made me nervous. That's simply my story, not medical advice, but it taught me to ask questions before deciding what was possible for me. With my second pregnancy, my midwife suggested I take my blood pressure at home every morning. I did, and it was completely normal. With my first baby, that high blood pressure was one of the reasons I was induced. So if blood pressure comes up for you, talk to your midwife about checking it at home, where you're relaxed.

So don't rule yourself out too fast. A breech baby or twins don't automatically take a home or birth-center birth off the table to talk about. Some experienced midwives can talk through your options with you, like trying to turn a breech baby before labor. I knew women at my birth center who had twins. Just talk to your midwife. Ask if she has experience with twins or breech babies.

Your due date is just a guess

My midwives could not care less about my due date. From the very beginning they told me the baby comes when the baby comes. So you have a birth month, but the exact day doesn't really matter. Hospitals often treat that date like a ticking clock. As you get close, they want you to come in, and if you go a day past it, everyone gets worried, and that can make you nervous too. With midwives, you just wait for your baby.

What a transfer usually looks like

Your midwives know if something is off, and they have a plan to get you to the hospital. If plans change, your midwife comes with you and shares your notes. They've cared for many, many first-time moms, and the plan is the same for everyone.

Did you know? 🌿 No clock on the cord. You wait for your baby, not a schedule. Many home birth midwives wait to clamp the cord until it stops pulsing on its own. That's often a few minutes, sometimes much longer, with no clock to rush it. It's something to see. Wherever you give birth, you can ask about delayed cord clamping and add it to your birth plan.

Ways to find comfort

Remember Day 1? When you're scared, your body tenses up, and that makes labor harder. When you feel calm and cared for, your body can relax and do its work. Here's what helps:

Warm water. A birth pool or bath.
Movement. Swaying, walking, leaning over a ball or the bed.
Calm birth breathing. Slow breaths, long on the exhale, practiced for weeks before so your body knows them.
Touch and sound. Massage, counter-pressure on your lower back, low humming, a soft, loose jaw.
Laughter and love. Ina May noticed that laughter and affection help labor flow. They really are part of the toolkit!

None of this has to wait until the big day. My midwives helped me practice it for months, the way an athlete trains for a race, and for me that made it pain, but not suffering.

Today's practice: breathe in for 4, out for 6, and let your jaw go loose. Do it for two minutes tonight before sleep. A tip someone once gave me that I still use, even now that I'm not pregnant: practice a few slow breaths every time you stop at a red traffic light while driving.

With love,Sybille 🤍

## The question no one asked me before my first birth
URL: https://borninthenest.com/lessons/day-5.html
Lesson 5 of 5 from Born in the Nest: A simple comparison, the questions to ask, and what comes next.

Lesson 5 of 5 · Home birth, explained by a mom who's done it
🌱The question no one asked me before my first birth
A simple comparison, the questions to ask, and what comes next.

Before my first birth, no one ever asked me the most important question: Where do you want to give birth? I didn't even know it was a choice.

You made it to Day 5! Here's the big idea one more time: you have a choice, and your body does its best work where you feel calm and loved.

Your three options, simply

🏡 Home birth: your own bed, your own space, a midwife who knows you, and the people you love right beside you. Your midwife always has a plan if you ever need the hospital, but most of the time you get to stay right where you are, at home. Your team knows you and your baby inside and out, and they're with you during the birth.

🌿 Birth center: a calm, home-like place made just for giving birth, with comfy beds, birth tubs and midwives who know you. Your family is welcome, and you can move, eat and rest the way your body wants. Your team knows you and your baby inside and out, and they're with you during the birth.

🏥 Hospital: if a hospital is the place where you feel most relaxed, that's wonderful, go there. If you're not sure yet, take your time, meet a few midwives, and see what feels right before you decide. Staff work in shifts, so you'll likely meet completely different people, and it may not be your own doctor.

Your first steps

Find a midwife, birth center or hospital. The internet and AI are your friends here. Search online or ask an AI assistant for midwives, birth centers and hospitals near you, and read what other moms say in their reviews.
Book a consultation with two or three. Most offer one.
Notice how you feel. Pay attention to your very first feelings when you walk in, and to the people you meet and talk with. Do you feel loved, calm and heard? If you can't be yourself, can't ask any question you want, or feel pushed into certain things, that's a red flag, and you should pay attention to it.
Ask your questions.Notice how you feel. This is the most important one. When you take your first step into the birth center or the office, do you feel calm? Do you feel like you'd love to hang out there and just be around your midwives, without even having to talk? That's the feeling we're going for. Then you can ask all the other questions.
Ask what they know about nutrition, sleep and wellbeing. Good pregnancy care is more than checkups. It includes how you eat, how you sleep and how you feel. Fueling your body is one of the most important things you can do during pregnancy, so your midwives should know a lot about it. If they can't really talk about nutrition, sleep and wellbeing, they're probably not the best fit.
How many births have you attended, and what's your training?
How do you prepare women for birth?
What nutrition and lifestyle advice do you give during pregnancy?
What does labor actually feel like when I'm not numb?
Who's your backup, and who comes with you to births?
What happens if I need to transfer to a hospital, and which hospital do you use?
What equipment and medicines do you bring?
How will my partner be part of it?
What does it cost, and does my insurance cover a birth center or home birth?
Do I have to decide right now, or when?

When you're ready to read more: Here are my favorite books, the ones that truly helped me. I love them, and I'll read them again. Ina May's Guide to Childbirth and Spiritual Midwifery by Ina May Gaskin (her famous reminder: "your body is not a lemon"), HypnoBirthing: The Mongan Method by Marie Mongan, and The Heart in the Womb by Dr. Amali Lokugamage, an obstetrician's look at love and birth. Ina May's books include many detailed birth stories, so skip any that feel like too much.

Short on time? I've got you. I'll be doing a deep dive into each of these books in my weekly letter, with the most important takeaways, in case you don't have time to read them all.

With love from my nest to yours,Sybille 🤍

## About Sybille · Born in the Nest
URL: https://borninthenest.com/about.html
Hi, I'm Sybille, a mom of two. My first baby was born in a hospital and my second at home. Why I created Born in the Nest.

About
Hi, I'm Sybille

My mission: that every woman knows she has a choice in where and how she gives birth, and feels calm, loved and prepared, whatever she chooses.

I'm a mom of two. My first baby was born in a hospital: I was induced early and had an epidural. Labor lasted nearly two and a half days. I was completely numb, and I felt helpless. After I gave birth, I was drained of energy. What I needed was food, rest, and quiet. My second was born at home, in my own bed, with a midwife I trusted, and that birth showed me how calm and beautiful giving birth can be. Same body, completely different birth. The biggest difference was where I was and how calm and loved I felt.

As my midwife always said, pregnant women need to feel loved. She made me feel so special, and she told me how amazing our bodies are.

That's what Born in the Nest is about.

My midwives felt a little like superheroes to me. They paid attention to everything: what I was eating, how I was sleeping, how I was really feeling, and the small things I'd never have thought to mention. Often they seemed to understand what I needed just by looking at me, before I said a word.

My confidence didn't come all at once. At the start of my second pregnancy, I didn't have it yet. First I knew I didn't want another hospital birth. The decision for a home birth came later. Confidence grew month by month, through monthly visits with my midwives, then weekly ones near the end, books (Ina May Gaskin helped) and hypnobirthing practice. By month eight, I trusted my body more than I ever had.

Why Born in the Nest exists

No one told me I had another option until my second pregnancy. I want you to know sooner.

Many women think home birth is only for the craziest people. I'd love to change that. 😄

Choosing where to give birth, and finding the right midwife or birth center, are big decisions, and I wish I'd had someone I could count on when I made them. When I was pregnant, just a message from one of my midwives could calm me down and make my whole day feel lighter. That's what I want Born in the Nest to be for you: a warm, trusted place you can come back to whenever you need it.

It isn't a one-time thing. The five short lessons are right here on the site, for anyone, no signup needed. And if you'd like, I'll send you a weekly letter every Sunday, matched to your due month, the way a loving midwife would walk beside you. You're never alone on this journey. Think of it as a steady hand with you every week, all the way to the day you meet your baby.

Your options
You have more choices than you think.

Most of us grow up picturing just one way to have a baby. Many women never hear that, alongside a hospital, they can also choose a birth center or a home birth with a midwife. Born in the Nest opens that door, so you can see every option and choose what feels right for you. No pressure, no lectures, just possibilities (and maybe a snack).

Your birth options, explained →
Get the weekly letter

Home birth, honestly

A few myths, untangled.

MythHome birth is only for a certain kind of mom.
FactHome birth is for any mom who wants to feel calm and at home. Moms from all walks of life choose it.

MythYou don't have a say in where you give birth.
FactYou can choose wherever you want to give birth. It's your choice.

MythWithout a hospital, I'm not safe.
FactYour body has done this for centuries. And you're not alone: you have a team around you that has been with you for the past nine months and knows you and your baby inside and out. They'll know if something is off.

MythBirth is only about pain.
FactYes, there will be some pain, but birth isn't only about pain. Your body is made to do this. Labor comes in waves and builds up slowly, and between contractions you get real breaks to rest and breathe. Nature doesn't want you to suffer.

Why so many moms love giving birth at home

It's your own nest. It's not just your bed and your snacks. It's your food, your space, and everyone you love right around you. And after you give birth, you never have to leave.

The right midwife makes you feel calm, heard and loved, right from the first moment. That's how you should feel.

## Weekly pregnancy letter, every Sunday · Born in the Nest
URL: https://borninthenest.com/letters.html
A weekly letter every Sunday of your pregnancy, matched to your due month: one honest moment, one calm idea and one small step.

Every Sunday, matched to your due month
💌The weekly letter

One short, loving letter every Sunday of your pregnancy, matched to your due month, all the way to the day you meet your baby. Each one has three little parts:

One honest momentA real moment from my pregnancies, the sweet and the slightly ridiculous.

One calm ideaSomething worth knowing for right where you are, explained in everyday English.

One small stepA tiny thing to try this week. Five minutes, tops. Snacks optional.

The five lessons aren't in the letter. They're right here on the site, whenever you want them: read the five short lessons.

🪺The first letter is still warming up in the nest.
Each new letter will be gathered here, so you can come back to them anytime.

## Privacy · Born in the Nest
URL: https://borninthenest.com/privacy.html
How Born in the Nest handles your information, in plain English: what we collect (just your email, due month and first name), why, and how to unsubscribe.

Privacy
Your privacy, in plain English
Short, honest, and no fine-print surprises.

Last updated: October 29, 2026

Who we are

Born in the Nest is a small guide to birth choices, run by HyperLaunch LLC. If you ever have a question about your privacy, write to me at hello@borninthenest.com. I read every message.

What we collect

Only what you give us when you sign up: your email address, your due month and, if you'd like, your first name. That's it.

Why we collect it

To send you what you asked for: the weekly letter, every Sunday of your pregnancy, matched to your due month. Your due month is how we match each letter to where you are. If you share your first name, we use it to say hello properly. The five short lessons are on the site, so you don't need to share anything to read them.

We never sell or share your information

Not with advertisers, not with anyone. Your details are used only to send you Born in the Nest emails.

The services we use

Kit (formerly ConvertKit) sends our emails and keeps your email address, due month and first name secure for us. Like most email services, Kit can tell us whether an email was opened or a link was clicked, which helps us write emails that are actually useful. Kit doesn't sell your information. You can read Kit's privacy policy and how Kit handles subscriber data.

GitHub Pages hosts this website. Like any web host, GitHub may keep basic technical logs (such as IP addresses) to keep the site secure and running. Here's GitHub's privacy statement.

No tracking cookies

This website doesn't use analytics, advertising or tracking cookies. Even our fonts are hosted on our own site, so your visit isn't shared with font services. If that ever changes, we'll update this page first.

Unsubscribe anytime

Every email has an unsubscribe link at the bottom. One click and you're off the list, no hard feelings. You can also write to us anytime to ask what we have about you, to correct it, or to delete it, and we'll take care of it.

Education only

Born in the Nest shares education only. It isn't medical advice and doesn't replace care from your midwife or doctor. Please talk to your provider about anything health-related.

If this page changes

We'll update the date at the top of this page.

With love from my nest to yours,Sybille 🤍

## A sample weekly letter (weeks 20–24) · Born in the Nest
URL: https://borninthenest.com/sample-letter.html
A sample of the Born in the Nest weekly letter for weeks 20–24 of pregnancy: what's happening now, what to focus on and questions for your care team.

A sample of the weekly letter
💌Halfway there 🌸
What a weekly letter looks like, written for around weeks 20–24.

A sample letter. Every Sunday's letter is matched to where you are in your pregnancy, and this one is written for around weeks 20–24.

SubjectHalfway there 🌸 (and a word about marathons)

Hi there,

You're around weeks 20–24 now. Halfway! 🌸 In case no one has told you yet this week: you're doing beautifully.

🏡 One honest moment

While I was giving birth to my second child and the contractions started getting stronger, a moment of fear showed up. My midwife was pressing my hips, my hypnobirthing tracks were playing, and I blurted out, "I'm not a marathon runner!"

My husband said, "You totally are. You trained for this."

He was right, in the kindest way. I've never run a marathon. But for about four months before my second child was born, I practiced breathing through each wave. Small, quiet practice, again and again, until my body knew it by heart. When the big day came, it was there for me.

Here's a tip someone once gave me: practice your breathing every time you stop at a red traffic light while driving. I loved it, and I still do it today, even though I'm not pregnant. It's just practice, practice, practice. And once you get the hang of it, you can do it anywhere.

So this letter is about training. The soft kind. No running shoes required.

🌱 What's happening around now

Little flutters. Many women start to feel their baby move somewhere around now: tiny bubbles, taps or flutters. With a first baby it often comes a little later, and every pregnancy has its own timing.
The anatomy scan. Many women are offered a detailed ultrasound, often called the anatomy scan, somewhere around weeks 18–22. It can feel exciting and a little nerve-racking at the same time. Both are okay.
A bit more energy. Many women find this middle stretch of pregnancy brings some energy back. If that's you, enjoy it. If it isn't, rest is part of the training too.

💛 What to focus on this week

Two minutes of breathing. Tonight before sleep, breathe in for 4 and out for 6, and let your jaw go loose. That's it. You're not doing it for tonight. You're doing it for the day you meet your baby.
Fuel and move in a way you enjoy. The day my second child was born looked completely ordinary: coffee, my weekly 45-minute walk, lunch, my daily stretches. (And a steak dinner. About five minutes later it was go time. Zero regrets. 🥩) Ask your midwife or doctor what movement and food look like for your pregnancy, then find a version that feels good.

🩺 Questions worth asking your midwife or doctor

What will you look at during my anatomy scan, and what happens next if anything needs a closer look?
What kind of movement and exercise feels right for my pregnancy right now?
What does good fuel look like for me these days, and is there anything you'd like me to keep an eye on?
When should I start practicing breathing or relaxation for birth, and are there classes you'd recommend?

My midwives paid attention to everything: what I was eating, how I was sleeping, how I was really feeling. So bring all of it to your next visit. And the advice I'd give my first-time self: if something feels off, even if you can't put it into words yet, pause. Write it down. Ask questions.

Pregnancy comes with a lot of decisions, big and small, for you and your baby. The best advice I can give you: sit on it. You don't have to decide in that second. Take it home, breathe into it, let it settle. And like I said, if something feels off, pause, write it down and ask more questions.

💌 Coming next week

Your birth preferences: what matters most to you, and a calm "if plans change" page.

Until then, hit reply and tell me: have you felt those first little flutters yet? I read every message.

With love from my nest to yours,Sybille 🤍Mom of two · Chief Nest Officer, Born in the Nest

Education only, not medical advice. Always talk with your midwife or doctor about your own pregnancy.
